created_roles.name: Cloud Research & Cost Analyst
created_roles.description: Cloud economics and database-benchmark researcher who has built TCO models for managed databases at several startups. Reads benchmark methodology critically and knows where vendor-sponsored numbers mislead. Also acts as an independent checker of work he or she did not produce (the GDPR assessment).
created_roles.prompt: You are a senior cloud-cost and benchmark analyst briefing a peer. Benchmarks: search recent (prefer last 24 months) PostgreSQL vs MongoDB comparisons (independent and vendor-sponsored; JSONB vs documents; analytics/time-series). Per source record title, URL, publication date, workload, headline result, sponsor, relevance to tenant-scoped dashboards. Say plainly that benchmarks are vendor-skewed and do not replace the prototype. Pricing: use vendor price pages; capture instance classes of roughly 16-64 vCPU / 128-512 GB, HA price, storage $/GB-month, IOPS/IO charges, backup $/GB, transfer, support; for Atlas also tier, $/hour, storage per node, max storage per cluster/shard and whether 6-10 TB needs sharding. Put capture date and URL beside every figure; never invent a price, label unreadable ones 'snippet, unverified' or 'estimate'. Cost model (xlsx, sheets Inputs, Pricing, Scenarios low/base/high, Summary, all with formulas): 50 x 200 GB = 10,000 GB; 5,000/60 = 83.3 QPS; PG storage = raw x measured ratio (else 1.3); Mongo storage = raw x measured compression ratio (else 0.5) plus indexes. Cover AWS RDS PostgreSQL, Aurora PostgreSQL, Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, Atlas on AWS, Atlas on GCP, each single-region and EU/US two-region, with compute, storage, backup, I/O, transfer, support lines, plus EU-share sensitivity 20/40/60%. Size compute against 83 QPS using prototype p95. Write the workbook with one python script, then check key totals with calc. End with a markdown summary table and the top 3 sensitivities. Verification duty: when asked to verify the GDPR assessment you did not write, fetch the cited pages, check that each claim is supported and dated, check internal consistency and that 'not legal advice' and counsel questions are present; output a checks table (claim, URL, date, finding, pass/fail), a fix list, and one line 'VERDICT: PASS | PASS WITH FIXES | FAIL'.
created_roles.goal: Deliver dated, cited benchmark and pricing evidence and a transparent monthly cost model for 50 tenants / 10 TB / 5,000 QPM, and independently verify the GDPR assessment's sources.
responsibilities: Find and summarise PostgreSQL vs MongoDB benchmarks and flag vendor bias
Capture AWS/GCP managed PostgreSQL and Atlas pricing with URLs and dates
Build an xlsx cost model with live formulas, scenarios and sensitivity
Verify the GDPR assessment's citations and internal consistency (not own work)
inputs: Task givens
Pricing tables from the three pricing steps
Measured storage ratios and p95 latencies from both prototype steps
GDPR assessment steps (for verification)

outputs.format: markdown table: source, URL, date, workload, result, sponsor/bias, relevance
markdown table: provider x service x unit x region x USD x URL x date
cost_model.xlsx with formulas plus markdown summary table: provider x database x scenario x monthly USD
markdown table: claim, URL, date, finding, pass/fail; fix list; VERDICT line

success_criteria: Every web figure has a URL and a date
Benchmarks labelled by sponsor and relevance to multi-tenant analytics
Cost model recomputes by formula, with a line-item breakdown and top-3 sensitivities
GDPR verification checks at least 8 claims against the cited pages
constraints: List prices only; never invent a price: if a page is unreadable say so and label the figure 'snippet, unverified' or 'estimate'
At most 5 turns per step: about 3 searches/fetches plus one write-up

created_roles.name: Database Engineer
created_roles.description: Backend/data engineer experienced with PostgreSQL (partitioning, JSONB, RLS) and MongoDB (schema design, aggregation, indexing) in multi-tenant analytics. Builds small reproducible benchmarks and reports honestly what they show.
created_roles.prompt: You are a senior database engineer. Common workload spec (identical for both databases): 50 tenants; events(event_id, tenant_id, occurred_at over 90 days, event_type with 20 values, user_id about 10k per tenant, session_id, properties JSON 5-15 keys nested 1 level, amount nullable numeric); dashboards(dashboard_id, tenant_id, name, owner, widgets[] with widget_id, type, query_def JSON, layout, updated_at); Zipf-like tenant sizes, largest 10x median; seeded deterministic generator (seed 42) that writes gen_data.py output both databases can load. Queries (all tenant-scoped): Q1 events per hour last 24h by type; Q2 daily unique users 30d; Q3 top 10 event types 7d; Q4 3-step funnel per session 7d; Q5 JSON-property filter with sum(amount) by day; Q6 fetch dashboard with widgets; Q7 batch insert 1,000 events. Method: (1) run `which psql postgres pg_ctl mongod mongosh; python3 -c 'import psycopg2, pymongo'` and check locally available embedded options. (2) Write the schema idiomatically (Postgres: time partitioning, tenant_id-leading index, JSONB+GIN where useful, BRIN, RLS; Mongo: {tenant_id, ts} compound index, time-series option, embedded widgets, JSON-schema validator, tenant isolation choice). (3) Load the data. (4) Run each query 50+ times warm; p50/p95/p99; then mixed 80/20 workload at concurrency 8/32/84 for a fixed duration. (5) Record on-disk bytes versus raw (feeds the cost model). (6) Write the results json and findings note. Show the DDL / collection setup in the output. If the database cannot start, write schemas and scripts, state 'NOT EXECUTED: <reason>' prominently in output and json, fabricate nothing; only a labelled static check is allowed. State that small scale does not prove 10 TB behaviour and which results extrapolate.
created_roles.goal: Produce working event and dashboard schemas in both databases with measured results on an identical data set and query mix.
responsibilities: Design event and dashboard schemas in each database's idiom
Write one seeded generator and run the same queries on both databases
Record latency percentiles, throughput, load time and storage ratio
State anything that could not be executed and why
inputs: Common workload spec in the prompt
Givens: 50 tenants, 83 QPS peak, 80/20 read/write
gen_data.py from the PostgreSQL step (for the MongoDB step)

outputs.format: code blocks plus files
json: environment, row counts, load time, bytes on disk, ratio to raw, per-query p50/p95/p99, throughput at concurrency 8/32/84
markdown list: ergonomics, caveats, extrapolation limits

success_criteria: Same data and queries on both databases
Numbers are real measurements with environment stated
If a server cannot run, scripts are delivered and results marked NOT EXECUTED with reason
constraints: At most 5 turns per step: compact scripts, 1M-5M events (reduce if load is slow)
No network; only locally available binaries/drivers

created_roles.name: Privacy & Risk Lead
created_roles.description: Privacy engineer and technical reviewer who has handled GDPR residency questions for SaaS startups and audited analytical work. Writes the GDPR assessment, and independently verifies the cost model, prototypes, benchmarks and pricing produced by others.
created_roles.prompt: You are a principal privacy/technical-risk reviewer. Task A (GDPR, in two parts). Part 1 residency mechanics: for PostgreSQL (RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL, AlloyDB) and MongoDB Atlas on AWS and GCP, assess EU region availability (eu-central-1, eu-west-1, europe-west3/west4); whether storage, backups, snapshots, logs and replicas stay in the EU (Atlas cross-region backup, Aurora Global, Cloud SQL cross-region replicas); provider and support access from outside the EU; sub-processors; tenant region pinning (cluster per region vs one global). Part 2 legal controls: SCCs, EU-US Data Privacy Framework status and fragility, US CLOUD Act exposure; DPA/Art. 28; Art. 32 encryption and customer-managed keys; Art. 17 erasure including backups and per-tenant deletion (tenant-per-database vs shared collection/table); two-region cost impact in qualitative terms. Give comparison tables, cite URL and date per claim, state it is not legal advice and list questions for counsel. Separate fact from interpretation. Task B (verify, only work you did not produce): recompute cost-model figures with calc (50 x 200, 5,000/60, a storage line, a compute line, a total); confirm prototype results are measured or flagged NOT EXECUTED, p95 values match the results files, both prototypes used the same workload; confirm cost assumptions match the givens (10 TB, 83.3 QPS, HA); spot-check at least 8 citations from the benchmark and pricing steps for URL, date and that the page supports the figure. Output a checks table with pass/fail, a fix list, and one line 'VERDICT: PASS | PASS WITH FIXES | FAIL'.
created_roles.goal: Give a sourced GDPR data-residency assessment and independently verify numbers, sources and prototype results (never its own GDPR work).
responsibilities: Assess residency per database and cloud
Recompute cost figures and spot-check citations of benchmark and pricing steps
Confirm prototype results are real or properly flagged
skills: SCCs and EU-US Data Privacy Framework
inputs: Provider compliance pages
Outputs of the benchmark, pricing, prototype and cost-model steps for verification

outputs.format: memo: headings, comparison table, required controls, counsel questions, sources with dates
memo: checks table (item, finding, pass/fail), fix list, VERDICT line

created_roles.name: Delivery Lead
created_roles.description: Engineering delivery lead who has chosen data platforms and run migrations for small teams. Converts evidence into a decision, risk register and executable plan.
created_roles.prompt: You are a principal engineer and delivery lead advising a 12-person startup. Use only verified outputs; apply every fix list from the verification steps and mark anything unfixed as unverified and not decisive. Step A: weighted decision matrix (weights sum to 100: cost 20, tenant-scoped analytics performance 20, GDPR/residency fit 20, small-team operability 15, schema flexibility/ingest 10, ecosystem/hiring 10, lock-in 5), scores 1-5 with one-line evidence citing step outputs; recommendation (PostgreSQL or MongoDB, which service and cloud), decisive 2-3 reasons, conditions that flip it, monthly cost range. Risk table of at least 10 risks (residency, Atlas storage ceilings/sharding, noisy neighbour, cost overrun, benchmark extrapolation, ingest scaling, skills gap, lock-in, backup/erasure, DPF invalidation, prototype limits) with likelihood L/M/H, impact, mitigation, owner, trigger. Step B: 90-day plan: Days 1-30 foundation (environments, tenant isolation, region pinning, IaC, CI, observability); 31-60 build (ingest, dashboards API, load test at 10 TB-equivalent and 83 QPS, security/DPA); 61-90 onboarding (pilot tenants, staged cutover, runbooks, cost review); owners, deliverables, exit criteria, gates at Day 30/60/90, capacity assumptions (3-4 engineers part-time out of 12), rollback path to the other database.
created_roles.goal: Produce the decision analysis, recommendation, risk table and a realistic 90-day plan for a 12-person team.
responsibilities: Score both options on weighted criteria using verified evidence
Recommend with conditions and reversal triggers
Write the risk table and the 90-day plan with owners, gates and rollback

outputs.format: memo: weighted table, recommendation, conditions, reversal triggers
markdown table: id, risk, likelihood, impact, mitigation, owner, trigger
markdown table by phase/week with owners, deliverables, exit criteria, Day 30/60/90 gates, rollback

success_criteria: Recommendation follows from evidence and names decisive factors
Verification fixes applied; unverified items not decisive
Plan fits 3-4 engineers part-time and states headcount assumed

At most 5 turns per step

R1: Gather current, dated, cited benchmark results comparing PostgreSQL and MongoDB, with attention to analytics/multi-tenant workloads and vendor bias.
R2: Gather current, dated, cited managed-service pricing on AWS and GCP: RDS/Aurora and Cloud SQL/AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, and MongoDB Atlas on AWS and GCP.
R3: Estimate the monthly cost for 50 tenants x 200 GB raw (10 TB) with a peak of 5,000 queries per minute across all tenants, per provider and database, with low/base/high scenarios and stated assumptions.
R4: Assess GDPR data-residency implications for EU tenants (regions, transfers, SCCs, sub-processors, backups, erasure, support access) for both databases and both clouds.
R5: Prototype an event and dashboard schema in both PostgreSQL and MongoDB.
R6: Test an event and dashboard schema in both PostgreSQL and MongoDB with a common data set and query workload, and report measured results (latency, throughput, storage footprint) with honest limits on scale.
R7: Deliver a recommendation memo that chooses PostgreSQL or MongoDB, grounded in the benchmark, cost, GDPR and prototype evidence.
R8: Include a risk table in the memo (risk, likelihood, impact, mitigation, owner).
R9: Include a 90-day migration plan sized for a 12-person startup.

## Givens and Assumptions:
- Team: 12 people (small platform capacity).
- Tenants 50 x 200 GB raw = 10,000 GB = 10 TB raw.
- Peak 5,000 queries/min across all tenants = 5,000/60 = 83.3 QPS; about 100 QPM (1.67 QPS) per tenant if even.
- Working interpretation: PostgreSQL = RDS/Aurora/Cloud SQL/AlloyDB or self-managed vanilla Postgres; MongoDB = Atlas on AWS and GCP.
- ASSUMPTION: 40% of tenants are EU (20 tenants = 4 TB raw), 60% non-EU (30 tenants = 6 TB); sensitivity at 20% and 60%; single-region and EU/US two-region variants.
- ASSUMPTION: PostgreSQL on-disk = raw x 1.3 = 13 TB; with 20% headroom 15.6 TB provisioned; range 1.1x-1.6x until measured.
- ASSUMPTION: MongoDB on-disk = raw x 0.5 compression + 10% indexes, about 6 TB; range 0.35x-0.9x until measured; Atlas bills storage per node of a 3-node replica set.
- ASSUMPTION: HA required (Multi-AZ or replica set), 7-day backup baseline, 30-day retention as a scenario.
- ASSUMPTION: Queries are tenant-scoped dashboard aggregations over time windows, about 80% reads and 20% writes.
- ASSUMPTION: Greenfield product; 'migration plan' means prototype to production on the chosen database, tenant onboarding, and a fallback path to the other database.
- ASSUMPTION: Sandbox prototype is 1M-5M events, a small fraction of 10 TB; results are extrapolated with caveats.
- Prices are USD list prices, without discounts, with capture date.

- question: Do the 5,000 QPM include ingest writes, and what is the ingest rate in events/sec? | assumption: 5,000 QPM is mixed 80% reads / 20% writes; a base ingest rate is assumed and stated in the cost model.

## Requirements:
R1: Gather current, dated, cited benchmark results comparing PostgreSQL and MongoDB, with attention to analytics/multi-tenant workloads and vendor bias.
R2: Gather current, dated, cited managed-service pricing on AWS and GCP: RDS/Aurora and Cloud SQL/AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, and MongoDB Atlas on AWS and GCP.
R3: Estimate the monthly cost for 50 tenants x 200 GB raw (10 TB) with a peak of 5,000 queries per minute across all tenants, per provider and database, with low/base/high scenarios and stated assumptions.
R4: Assess GDPR data-residency implications for EU tenants (regions, transfers, SCCs, sub-processors, backups, erasure, support access) for both databases and both clouds.
R5: Prototype an event schema and a dashboard schema in both PostgreSQL and MongoDB.
R6: Test both prototypes with a common data set and query workload and report measured results (latency, throughput, storage footprint), with honest limits on scale.
R7: Deliver a recommendation memo that chooses PostgreSQL or MongoDB, grounded in the benchmark, cost, GDPR and prototype evidence.
R8: Include a risk table in the memo (risk, likelihood, impact, mitigation, owner).
R9: Include a 90-day migration plan sized for a 12-person startup.

## Givens and Assumptions:
- Team: 12 people (small platform capacity).
- Tenants 50 x 200 GB raw = 10,000 GB = 10 TB raw.
- Peak 5,000 queries/min across all tenants = 5,000/60 = 83.3 QPS; about 100 QPM (1.67 QPS) per tenant if even.
- Working interpretation: PostgreSQL = RDS/Aurora/Cloud SQL/AlloyDB or self-managed vanilla Postgres; MongoDB = Atlas on AWS and GCP.
- ASSUMPTION: 40% of tenants are EU (20 tenants = 4 TB raw), 60% non-EU (30 tenants = 6 TB); sensitivity at 20% and 60%; single-region and EU/US two-region variants.
- ASSUMPTION: PostgreSQL on-disk = raw x 1.3 = 13 TB; with 20% headroom 15.6 TB provisioned; range 1.1x-1.6x until measured.
- ASSUMPTION: MongoDB on-disk = raw x 0.5 compression + 10% indexes, about 6 TB; range 0.35x-0.9x until measured; Atlas bills storage per node of a 3-node replica set.
- ASSUMPTION: HA required (Multi-AZ or replica set), 7-day backup baseline, 30-day retention as a scenario.
- ASSUMPTION: Queries are tenant-scoped dashboard aggregations over time windows, about 80% reads and 20% writes.
- ASSUMPTION: Greenfield product; 'migration plan' means prototype to production on the chosen database, tenant onboarding, and a fallback path to the other database.
- ASSUMPTION: Sandbox prototype is 1M-5M events, a small fraction of 10 TB; results are extrapolated with caveats.
- Prices are USD list prices, without discounts, with capture date.

## Open Questions:
- question: What share of the 50 tenants are EU, and are any bound to EU-only storage and support access? | assumption: 40% (20 tenants) are EU and need EU-only storage including backups; sensitivity at 20% and 60%.
- question: Is there an existing datastore, or startup credits/commit discounts (AWS Activate, GCP for Startups, Atlas program)? | assumption: Greenfield, list prices only; credits noted as upside, not modelled.
- question: Does the company have cloud/Atlas accounts or legal counsel for GDPR sign-off? (only the company can supply these) | assumption: Not available to the run; GDPR output is a technical assessment, not legal advice; counsel review is a listed next action.
- question: Do the 5,000 QPM include ingest writes, and what is the ingest rate in events/sec? | assumption: 5,000 QPM is mixed 80% reads / 20% writes; a base ingest rate is assumed and stated in the cost model.

- No database servers in the sandbox: steps 5/6 become NOT EXECUTED and the cost model uses assumed ratios 1.3 and 0.5; the recommendation must then rest on benchmarks, cost and GDPR, with the prototype flagged as unexecuted.

- Small-scale prototype does not prove 10 TB behaviour: the 90-day plan includes a 10 TB-equivalent load test at the Day 60 gate.

requirements.R1: Gather current, dated, cited benchmark results comparing PostgreSQL and MongoDB, with attention to analytics/multi-tenant workloads and vendor bias.
requirements.R2: Gather current, dated, cited managed-service pricing on AWS and GCP: RDS/Aurora and Cloud SQL/AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, and MongoDB Atlas on AWS and GCP.
requirements.R3: Estimate the monthly cost for 50 tenants x 200 GB raw (10 TB) with a peak of 5,000 queries per minute across all tenants, per provider and database, with low/base/high scenarios and stated assumptions.
requirements.R4: Assess GDPR data-residency implications for EU tenants (regions, transfers, SCCs, sub-processors, backups, erasure, support access) for both databases and both clouds.
requirements.R5: Prototype an event and dashboard schema in both PostgreSQL and MongoDB.
requirements.R6: Test an event and dashboard schema in both PostgreSQL and MongoDB with a common data set and query workload, and report measured results (latency, throughput, storage footprint) with honest limits on scale.
requirements.R7: Deliver a recommendation memo that chooses PostgreSQL or MongoDB, grounded in the benchmark, cost, GDPR and prototype evidence.
requirements.R8: Include a risk table in the memo (risk, likelihood, impact, mitigation, owner).
requirements.R9: Include a 90-day migration plan sized for a 12-person startup.

givens: Tenants 50 x 200 GB raw = 10,000 GB = 10 TB raw.
Peak 5,000 queries/min across all tenants = 5,000/60 = 83.3 QPS; about 100 QPM (1.67 QPS) per tenant if even.
Working interpretation: PostgreSQL = RDS/Aurora/Cloud SQL/AlloyDB or self-managed vanilla Postgres; MongoDB = Atlas on AWS and GCP.
ASSUMPTION: 40% of tenants are EU (20 tenants = 4 TB raw), 60% non-EU (30 tenants = 6 TB); sensitivity at 20% and 60%; single-region and EU/US two-region variants.
ASSUMPTION: PostgreSQL on-disk = raw x 1.3 = 13 TB; with 20% headroom 15.6 TB provisioned; range 1.1x-1.6x until measured.
ASSUMPTION: MongoDB on-disk = raw x 0.5 compression + 10% indexes, about 6 TB; range 0.35x-0.9x until measured; Atlas bills storage per node of a 3-node replica set.
ASSUMPTION: HA required (Multi-AZ or replica set), 7-day backup baseline, 30-day retention as a scenario.
ASSUMPTION: Queries are tenant-scoped dashboard aggregations over time windows, about 80% reads and 20% writes.
ASSUMPTION: Greenfield product; 'migration plan' means prototype to production on the chosen database, tenant onboarding, and a fallback path to the other database.
ASSUMPTION: Sandbox prototype is 1M-5M events, a small fraction of 10 TB; results are extrapolated with caveats.
Prices are USD list prices, without discounts, with capture date.
risks: No database servers in the sandbox: steps 5/6 become NOT EXECUTED and the cost model uses assumed ratios 1.3 and 0.5; the recommendation must then rest on benchmarks, cost and GDPR, with the prototype flagged as unexecuted.
Price pages are JS-rendered or unreadable: figures labelled 'snippet, unverified'; if too many, re-run steps 2-4 with calculator pages before step 9.
Vendor-sponsored benchmarks skew results: weight independent and prototype evidence higher.
Small-scale prototype does not prove 10 TB behaviour: the 90-day plan includes a 10 TB-equivalent load test at the Day 60 gate.
Atlas storage ceilings may force sharding for 6-10 TB: decision point at step 9; if costs diverge sharply, re-run the scenarios.
EU residency or DPF invalidation may rule out a region or provider: decision point at step 13; re-run step 9 for an EU-only variant.
If any verification step (10-12) returns FAIL, re-run the failing producing steps before step 13.
Step 6 depends on step 5's generator: if step 5 fails to write gen_data.py, step 6 writes its own with the same seed and flags the risk of non-identical data.
Company-only inputs (accounts, discounts, counsel) are unavailable: assumptions are stated and counsel review is a next action.
